[p. 601]

The opening of the surah with *tabbat* (perished) suggests that it was revealed as rebuke and warning. This is a skilled opening (*bara'at al-istihlal*, the art of opening with a striking phrase), like the way satirical poems open with words that signal blame and abuse. From the same category is the Exalted One's saying: ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 1], as the surah that contains the warning against the defrauders opens with the word *waylun* (woe). From this same category is the verse of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hakam, one of the poets of the *Hamasah* (the Hamasah anthology of poetry):

May God curse Qays, Qays of 'Aylan, for they have neglected the frontiers of the Muslims and turned away.

And the line of Abu Tammam at the opening of a satire:

Fire, shame, what is hateful, and destruction.

From this Abu Bakr ibn al-Khazin took his line at the opening of an ode of congratulation on a birth:

Majshari, for fortune has fulfilled what it promised.

[p. 601]

*Al-tabb* means loss and ruin. The statement is an invocation and a reproach against Abu Lahab, by which God repelled from His Prophet the same kind of word with which Abu Lahab abused Muhammad (ﷺ), as a fitting recompense.

The attribution of *tabb* to the two hands is based on what is reported: when Abu Lahab said to the Prophet, "Perish you for the rest of the day! Is it for this that you gathered us?", he took up a stone to throw at him. It is also reported from Tariq al-Muharibi that he said: "While I was in the market of Dhu al-Majaz, I saw a young man saying, 'O people, say there is no god but God and you will prosper,' and behind him a man was pelting him, his shins and heels bleeding, saying, 'O people, he is a liar, so do not believe him.' I asked, 'Who is this?' They said, 'This is Muhammad, who claims to be a prophet, and this is his uncle Abu Lahab.'" So the invocation fell upon his hands, because they were the cause of the harm done to the Prophet (ﷺ), just as one says to someone who utters something hateful, "Stones in your mouth, or dust in your mouth," and as al-Nabigha said:

Sitting by their tents, they cast dust upon them, may God throw into those hands the calamities.

The opposite is said to one who speaks a good word: "May your mouth not be broken." An Arab of the Banu Asad said:

I called upon Miswar when a calamity befell me, so may the hands of Miswar answer, answer!

For he called him to help against the enemy who had attacked him, and help comes through the action of the hand, by striking or thrusting.

Abu Lahab is 'Abd al-'Uzza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, the uncle of the Prophet (ﷺ). His kunya (teknonym) was Abu 'Utbah, after his son. As for his kunya Abu Lahab in the verse, it is said that he was called by it in the pre-Islamic period "for his beauty and the brightness of his face," and that he became famous by that kunya, as the report of Tariq al-Muharibi indicates. A similar report is from Rabi'ah ibn 'Abbad al-Dili in the *Musnad* of Ahmad. The Qur'an named him by his kunya rather than his name, either because his name contained the worship of al-'Uzza, which the Qur'an does not approve, or because he was better known by his kunya than by his proper name, or because his kunya allows a meaning that points to his destiny of going to the Fire. This is a metonymy for his being a dweller of Hell, since *lahab* is the flames of fire when they blaze and the smoke departs from them. *Ab* (father) is applied to one who is constantly attached to what is attributed to him, as in the saying "her father and her measurer" [i.e., the one who measures out for her]. Likewise Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was given the kunya "father of guests," and the Prophet (ﷺ) gave the kunya Abu Hurayrah to 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sakhr al-Dawsi, because he carried a kitten in the sleeve of his shirt. The month of Ramadan was given the kunya "father of blessings," and the wolf was given the kunya "father of Ja'dah," and *al-Ja'dah* is a young goat, because the wolf is constantly pursuing it to devour it. So the kunya of Abu Lahab was apt and fitting for his condition, in that he deserved the flame of Hell. This interpretation thus becomes a metonymy for his being a dweller of Hell, so that the sense moves from "Abu Lahab" meaning "one constantly attached to the flame" to the consequence of that constant attachment in common usage, namely that he is one of the people of Hell. This is an assumed (*ideal*) attachment, based on optimism drawn from names and the like, as al-Taftazani indicated in the section on proper nouns in his commentary on *al-Miftah*, and he quoted the verse of the poet:

I aimed at Abu al-Mahasin that I might see him, out of a longing that drew me to him.
When I saw him, I saw him alone, and I did not see among his sons any son with him.

It may also be that the kunya of Abu Lahab is *al-Hatab* (firewood), as is indicated by what is reported from Abu Hurayrah: "The daughter of Abu Lahab said to the Prophet (ﷺ), 'People shout at me and say, "I am the daughter of the firewood of the Fire."'" The hadith [continues].

The reciters: the majority read the word *Lahab* with a fatha on the *ha'*, while Ibn Kathir read it with a sukun on the *ha'*. This is a dialectal form, because the Arabs often make the middle consonant of a word with a vowel quiescent when it follows a *fa'*. It may also be that *Lahab* had become part of a proper name, and the Arabs sometimes change some of the vowels of a noun when they transfer it to use as a proper name, as they said *Shams* with a damma on the *shin*. This is also the case with Shams ibn Malik the poet, whom Ta'abbata Sharran mentioned in his verse:

Indeed I praise him and aim my praise at the son of the uncle of truth, Shams ibn Malik.

Abu al-Fath ibn Jinni said in *I'rab al-Hamasah* (grammatical analysis of the Hamasah): "It may be that the damma on the *shin* is in the manner of changing proper names, like Ma'd Yakrib, Tahlaka and Mawhab, and other things that were changed in the manner of their counterparts because of the newly acquired status of proper name." End of quote.

Likewise they said *Abu Sulma* with a damma on the *sin*, the kunya of the father of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma, because they transferred the name *Salma* with a fatha on the *sin*, from women's names, to make it the name of a man who is given it as a kunya, since they generally do not give kunyas with women's names.

[p. 603]

For this reason Ibn Kathir did not make the *ha'* quiescent in the Exalted One's saying ﴿of blazing flame﴾ [al-Masad: 3]. The reading of Ibn Kathir is the reading of the people of Mecca, so it may be that the kunya Abu Lahb with a sukun on the *ha'* was well known among them, to reflect how often it was used on people's tongues in his time.

The clause *wa tabba* (and he has perished) is either coordinated with the clause ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾, as a coordination of invocation upon invocation, if the attribution of perishing to the two hands is because they are the instrument of harm by throwing stones, as in the report of Tariq al-Muharibi. Thus the invocation is repeated upon his whole person, as a way of intensifying the insult and the reproach. By this it provides emphasis for the clause ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾, because it has the same meaning, and the two differ only in being general and particular. This difference is what requires its coordination; otherwise the emphasis would not be coordinated, because verbal emphasis is not joined with *wa* (and), as was mentioned earlier in the surah *al-Kafirun*.

Or it may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), with the *wa* being the *wa* of circumstance, and it is then not an invocation but an affirmation that what was invoked against him has occurred, like the saying of al-Nabigha:

May his Lord reward 'Adi ibn Hatim on my behalf with the reward of the snarling dogs.

And it has indeed been done. Thus the preceding statement is used for blame and gloating over him, or for seeking an increase. This reading is supported by the reading of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, "and he has indeed perished," so that the statement before it is purely for the sense of blame and contempt, rather than the sense of seeking the occurrence of his perishing. This is like the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah when he set out for the Battle of Mu'tah, in which he was martyred:

Until they say, when they pass by my grave: "May God guide you, a warrior, and he has indeed been guided."

Meaning: "and they say, 'and he has indeed been guided.'" So his words "May God guide you, a warrior" become purely a praise and an expression of envy for what he attained of martyrdom.

This is an excerpt from Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 111, verse 2:

﴿What his wealth and what he earned did not avail him.﴾

It is a resumptive initiating clause (isti'naf ibtida'i) marking the transition from the act of reviling and rebuking to informing that he is hopeless of salvation from this ruin, and that his wealth does not benefit him, nor does his earning; that is, that these do not avail him in warding off anything from him in the Hereafter.

صفحة ٦٠٤
The use of the past tense in His words "ma aghna" (did not avail) is to affirm that the non-availing has definitely occurred.
The "ma" is negative, and it may also be interrogative, for rebuke and denunciation.

Al-mal (wealth): property that is possessed and held as valuable. Among the Arabs its use came to be restricted to camels, and from the words of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): "Were it not for the wealth which I carry upon it in the way of Allah..." etc., regarding guarding against the supplication of the wronged, from the Muwatta', and Zuhayr said:

"Sound herds of wealth, looking out over Makhram"

The people of Madinah, Khaybar and Bahrain, however, use it predominantly for date palms. This has been discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, do not consume your wealth among yourselves unjustly﴾ [An-Nisa: 29] in Surat al-Baqarah and in other places.

﴿And what he earned﴾: "ma" is a relative pronoun with its relative clause, and the returning pronoun is omitted permissibly, since it is an accusative pronoun. The estimated sense is "and what he earned it," that is, what he gathered. What is meant by it is what he owns of other than livestock, such as money, weapons, real estate, goods and food. It is also permissible that by "his wealth" is meant all of his wealth, and the conjunction of "and what he earned" is a mention of the particular after the general, for the sake of emphasis on it; that is, what his inherited wealth (al-talid), which he inherited from his father 'Abd al-Muttalib, did not avail him, nor what he earned himself, which is his acquired wealth (al-tarif).

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that Abu Lahab said: "If what my nephew says is true, I will ransom myself on the Day of Resurrection with my wealth and my children." So Allah revealed: ﴿What his wealth and what he earned did not avail him.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "What he earned" is his child, for a child is part of a man's earnings.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 111, verse 3:

﴿He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame.﴾

It explains the phrase ﴿What his wealth availed him, nor what he gained﴾ [al-Masad: 2], meaning: nothing of the punishment of Jahannam (Hell) will be averted from him by anything. This Qur'an was revealed while Abu Lahab was still alive, and he died afterward in disbelief. Thus this verse was an announcement that he would not embrace Islam, and it was one of the signs of prophethood.

The sin (in sa-yasla) is for emphasis (tahqiq), like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord"﴾ [Yusuf: 98].

And yaslaa naran means he will be roasted by it and will feel its burning. The original form of the verb is salahu bi-l-nar, meaning he roasted him with the fire; then from it came Salia, like verbs of sensation such as fariha (to be happy) and marida (to be ill). The word (naran) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition.

Describing the fire as ﴿of blazing flame﴾ serves to strengthen the correspondence between his name and his disbelief, since he is Abu Lahab (Father of Flame) and the fire is of blazing flame.

This is what was alluded to earlier by mentioning his kunya (teknonym), as we mentioned just above; and in describing the fire by this there is an added revelation of the reality of the fire, and it is like emphasis.

Between the two words lahab (the first) and lahab (the second) there is a perfect paronomasia (jinas tamm).

[Page 605]

Having followed the censure and warning of Abu Lahab with a similar warning against his wife, because she shared in harming the Prophet ﷺ and helped him against him.

﴿And his wife, the carrier of firewood,﴾ ﴿with a rope of twisted fiber around her neck.﴾

*Wa-imra'atuhu* (his wife): that is, his spouse. God Most High said, in the story of Abraham, ﴿and his wife was standing﴾ [Hud: 71], and in the story of Lot, ﴿except his wife, who was among those who remained behind﴾, and in the story of Joseph, ﴿the wife of the Chief is seeking to seduce her young man from himself﴾ [Yusuf: 30].

The wife of Abu Lahab was Umm Jamil, whose name was Arwa bint Harb ibn Umayya, and she was the sister of Abu Sufyan ibn Harb. It was said that her name was *al-'Awra'* (the one-eyed or squint-eyed). It was said that this was a description, that she was blind in one eye, and it was said that it was her name. Some scholars mentioned that her name was *al-'Awwa'* with a hamza after the waw.

Umm Jamil used to carry thorny brushwood and thorns and place them at night on the path of the Prophet ﷺ by which he went to his house, in order to injure his feet.

When Abu Lahab received a threat derived from his kunya (teknonym), a threat whose wording was derived from his wife's own action, namely carrying firewood in this world, she was warned that she would carry firewood in Hell, to be kindled with it against her husband. That is a disgrace to her and to her husband, for God made the severity of his punishment come at the hands of the person most beloved to him, and made her the cause of the punishment of the person most dear to her.

[Page 606]

So His saying *wa-imra'atuhu* (and his wife) is coordinated with the hidden pronoun in *sa-yaslā* (he will burn), meaning: and his wife will burn in fire.

As for His saying ﴿carrier of firewood﴾, the majority of readers read *ḥammālata* in the nominative, as an attribute of his wife. It may be that this is her attribute in Hell, and it may be that it is the attribute by which she was known in this world, through bringing thornbrush firewood to place it on the path of the Prophet ﷺ. This is in the manner of allusion and indication to the reason for her punishment with that.

'Āṣim read *ḥammālata* in the accusative, as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of his wife. It contains the same allusion and indication as the nominative reading.

The clause ﴿with a rope of twisted fiber around her neck﴾ is a second attribute or a second circumstantial qualifier. It is an announcement of what she will be treated with in the Hereafter: a rope will be placed around her neck, with which she will carry firewood in Hell to feed the fire against her husband, as a recompense equal to her deed in this world, by which she angered God Most High.

*Al-jīd* means the neck. In usage it became specific to the neck of a woman and to the place of a necklace on it. Hence the neck is rarely mentioned in describing women in Arabic poetry, unless it is a neck described as beautiful. Imru' al-Qays combined the two in his saying:

*And a neck like the neck of a gazelle, not excessively long, when she displays it, nor left bare.*

Al-Suhayli said in *al-Rawḍ* (al-Rawḍ al-Unuf): "What is well known is that the neck is mentioned when ornament or beauty is mentioned. The mention of *al-jīd* here is appropriate by the rules of eloquence, because she is a woman, and women adorn their necks. Umm Jamil has no ornament in the Hereafter except the rope placed around her neck. So when that was established for her in place of ornament, the neck was mentioned along with it. Do you not see the saying of al-A'sha:

*On the day Qutayla reveals to us a neck, smooth and graceful, adorned with necklaces.*

He did not say 'a neck' (*'unuq*). And the saying of another:

*And finer than the necklace of the lovely one is her neck.*

He did not say 'her neck' (*'unuquhā*). Had he said it, it would have been insipid speech."

[Page 607]

I say: As for the saying of al-Ma'arri:

*The anklet is for the leg, and the lofty crown for what is above the head, and the string of pearls is for the neck.*

What made it pleasing is the paronomasia (*jinās*) between the necklace and the neck, to complete the assonance between *ḥajl* (anklet) and *rijl* (leg), and *tāj* (crown) and *ḥijāj* (forehead/head-covering). This is the poet's intended purpose.

*Al-ḥabl* (rope) is that by which things are tied together when one wants them joined to one another, and by which a beast or a prisoner is restrained so that it does not leave its place. It is a twisted cord of fiber or of leather thongs, of varying lengths according to the strength of what is bound or tied to a stake, a ring, or a tree, so that the one tied is prevented from leaving its place for another, to a distance intended. Ships' mooring ropes are also tied to the ground at the shores. It has been mentioned in His saying ﴿and hold fast to the rope of God, all together﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103], and His saying ﴿except by a rope from God and a rope from the people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 112], both in the Surah of Al 'Imran. It is said *ḥabalahu* when he tied it.

*Al-masad* is a strong fiber from Yemeni fiber, and the ropes twisted from it are strong and hard.

The predicate was placed first in His saying ﴿in her neck﴾, for the sake of emphasis on describing that dreadful state in which, in place of the necklace with which she used to adorn her neck in this world, a rope is placed around her neck, when she and her husband were among the wealthy and the chiefs of the people of al-Baṭḥā'. Umm Jamil died in polytheism.

[Page 608]

[Page 609]

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate

Surah al-Ikhlas

What is well known as its name, in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, in what came from his speech, and in most of what was narrated from the Companions, is (Surah *Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad*).

Al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Hurayra, and Ahmad related from Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari and from Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqba, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "*Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad* equals a third of the Qur'an." This is clear in that he intended to name it by that sentence, because of the feminine pronoun in his saying *(ta'dilu)* (equals), for it refers to it as a surah.

It has also been narrated from a group of Companions what indicates that it is named thus, so that is the name stated in the Sunna.

It is derived from al-Bukhari's hadith, from Ibrahim, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, what indicates that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "*Allahu al-Wahid al-Samad*, is a third of the Qur'an." He mentioned words differing from how it is recited, and its meaning is to be taken as intending the naming. al-Qurtubi mentioned that a man, whom he did not name, recited it in that way while people were listening, and claimed that what he recited was correct. al-Qurtubi censured him and reviled him.

It is named in most of the copies of the Qur'an (*maṣāḥif*), and in most of the exegeses, and in the *Jami'* of al-Tirmidhi, *Surat al-Ikhlas* (the Surah of Sincerity). This name became famous for its brevity and for gathering the meanings of this surah, because in it there is teaching people the sincerity of worship to God Most High, that is, the soundness of belief from associating others with God in divinity.

In some Tunisian copies of the Qur'an it is named *Surat al-Tawhid* (the Surah of Monotheism), because it includes the affirmation that He, Most High, is one.

In *al-Itqan* it is said that it is called *Surat al-Asas* (the Surah of the Foundation), because it includes the Unity of God, and that is

[Page 610]

the foundation of Islam. In *al-Kashshaf* (it was narrated from Ubayy and Anas, from the Prophet ﷺ, that "the seven heavens and the seven earths were founded upon *Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad*"), meaning: they were created only so that they would be signs of the Unity of God and knowledge of His attributes.

It is mentioned in *al-Kashshaf* that it and Surat al-Kafirun are called *al-Muqashqishatan*, that is, the two that free from polytheism and from hypocrisy.

al-Biqa'i in *Nazm al-Durar* named it *Surat al-Samad*, and this is among the names that al-Fakhr (al-Razi) gathered. Al-Fakhr, in *al-Tafsir al-Kabir*, devoted a section to the names of this surah, and mentioned for it twenty names, adding the title "Surah" to each name, and did not mention their chains of transmission. So you should trace them, though they vary. They are: *al-Tafrid* (the Isolation); *al-Tajrid* (the Stripping), because it mentions only His negative attributes, which are the attributes of majesty; *al-Tawhid* (the same reason); *al-Ikhlas* (for what we mentioned just above); *al-Najah* (the Deliverance), because it delivers from disbelief in this world and from the Fire in the Hereafter; *al-Wilaya* (the Guardianship), because whoever knows God by His oneness is among His believing friends who do not take as allies anyone other than God; *al-Nisba* (the Lineage), because it is said that it was revealed when the polytheists said: "Describe for us your Lord," as will come; *al-Ma'rifa* (the Knowledge), because it encompasses the attributes without which the knowledge of God is not complete; *al-Jamal* (the Beauty), because it gathers the roots of God's attributes, which are the most beautiful and most perfect attributes, and because it was narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "God is beautiful and loves beauty," so they asked him about that, and he said: "One, Eternal Refuge; He begets not, nor is He begotten." *Al-Muqashqisha* (it is said: *qashqasha al-dawa'u al-jarab* when the medicine cured the mange, because it cleanses from polytheism; it was previously mentioned that this is also a name of Surat al-Kafirun). *Al-Mu'awwidha* (because of the Prophet's ﷺ saying to 'Uthman ibn Maz'un when he was ill, and he sought refuge for him with it and with the two surahs after it, and said to him: "Seek refuge with them"). *Al-Samad* (because this word is specific to it). *Al-Asas* (because it is the foundation of the Islamic creed). *Al-Mani'a* (the Preventer), because it was narrated that it prevents the punishment of the grave and the blasts of the Fire. *Al-Mahdar* (the Attendance), because the angels attend to listen to it when it is recited. *Al-Munaffira* (the Repeller), because Satan flees at its recitation. *Al-Bara'a* (the Acquittal), because it acquits from polytheism. *Al-Mudhakkira* (the Reminder), because it recalls pure monotheism, which is deposited in the innate nature. *Al-Nur* (the Light), because it was narrated that the light of the Qur'an is *Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad*. *Al-Aman* (the Security), because whoever believes in what it contains is safe from punishment.

[Page 611]

With the addition of its well-known name (*Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad*), its names reach twenty-two. al-Firuzabadi said in *Basa'ir al-Tamyiz* that it is also called *al-Shafiya* (the Healing), which makes twenty-one names.

It is Meccan according to the majority. Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Abu al-'Aliya, and al-Qurazi said: it is Medinan. Both opinions are attributed to Ibn 'Abbas.

The source of this disagreement is the difference over its occasion of revelation. al-Tirmidhi related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, 'Ubayd al-'Attar related from Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu Ya'la related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that "the Quraysh said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'Describe your Lord for us.' So *Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad* was revealed to its end." On this basis it is Meccan.

Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas that "'Amir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad ibn Rabi'a, brother of Labid, came to the Prophet ﷺ. 'Amir said: 'To what do you call us?' He said: 'To God.' He said: 'Describe Him for us: is He of gold, or of silver, or of iron, or of wood?' (He supposed, out of ignorance, that God was an idol like their idols, made of metal, wood or stone.) So this surah was revealed." On this basis it is Medinan, because they came to him only after the Hijra.

al-Wahidi said that the rabbis of the Jews (among them Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf) said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Describe your Lord for us, perhaps we will believe in you," so it was revealed.

The correct view is that it is Meccan, for it gathers the root of monotheism, which is most of what was revealed of the Qur'an in Mecca. Perhaps the interpretation of those who said it was revealed when 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad asked, or when the rabbis of the Jews asked, is that the Prophet ﷺ recited this surah to them, and the narrator from the Ansar thought it was revealed at that moment, or the narrators did not record their statement with complete accuracy.

In *al-Itqan* it is said: "Some scholars reconciled the two reports by saying it was revealed more than once. Then it became clear to me that it is Medinan, as I explained in *Asbab al-Nuzul*." End of quote.

On the more correct view that it is Meccan, it is counted as the twenty-second surah in the order of revelation, revealed after Surat al-Nas and before Surat al-Najm.

[Page 612]

Its verses, according to the counting scholars of Medina, Kufa, and Basra, are four; according to the scholars of Mecca and Syria they are five, counting ﴿He begets not﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 3] as one verse and ﴿nor is He begotten﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 3] as another.

The affirmation of the Oneness of God Most High.

That none is sought for needs other than Him; His transcendence above the marks of created things; and the refutation that He could have a son.

And the refutation that the one who is born could be God, like Jesus, peace be upon him.

The hadiths on its virtues are numerous, and it is authentically established that it equals a third of the Qur'an. The interpretation of this hadith is mentioned in the commentaries on the *Muwatta'* and the *Two Sahihs*.

So His saying *wa-imra'atuhu* (and his wife) is coordinated with the hidden pronoun in *sa-yaslā* (he will burn), meaning: and his wife will burn in fire.

As for His saying ﴿carrier of firewood﴾, the majority of readers read *ḥammālata* in the nominative, as an attribute of his wife. It may be that this is her attribute in Hell, and it may be that it is the attribute by which she was known in this world, through bringing thornbrush firewood to place it on the path of the Prophet ﷺ. This is in the manner of allusion and indication to the reason for her punishment with that.

'Āṣim read *ḥammālata* in the accusative, as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of his wife. It contains the same allusion and indication as the nominative reading.

The clause ﴿with a rope of twisted fiber around her neck﴾ is a second attribute or a second circumstantial qualifier. It is an announcement of what she will be treated with in the Hereafter: a rope will be placed around her neck, with which she will carry firewood in Hell to feed the fire against her husband, as a recompense equal to her deed in this world, by which she angered God Most High.

*Al-jīd* means the neck. In usage it became specific to the neck of a woman and to the place of a necklace on it. Hence the neck is rarely mentioned in describing women in Arabic poetry, unless it is a neck described as beautiful. Imru' al-Qays combined the two in his saying:

*And a neck like the neck of a gazelle, not excessively long, when she displays it, nor left bare.*

Al-Suhayli said in *al-Rawḍ* (al-Rawḍ al-Unuf): "What is well known is that the neck is mentioned when ornament or beauty is mentioned. The mention of *al-jīd* here is appropriate by the rules of eloquence, because she is a woman, and women adorn their necks. Umm Jamil has no ornament in the Hereafter except the rope placed around her neck. So when that was established for her in place of ornament, the neck was mentioned along with it. Do you not see the saying of al-A'sha:

*On the day Qutayla reveals to us a neck, smooth and graceful, adorned with necklaces.*

He did not say 'a neck' (*'unuq*). And the saying of another:

*And finer than the necklace of the lovely one is her neck.*

He did not say 'her neck' (*'unuquhā*). Had he said it, it would have been insipid speech."

[Page 607]

I say: As for the saying of al-Ma'arri:

*The anklet is for the leg, and the lofty crown for what is above the head, and the string of pearls is for the neck.*

What made it pleasing is the paronomasia (*jinās*) between the necklace and the neck, to complete the assonance between *ḥajl* (anklet) and *rijl* (leg), and *tāj* (crown) and *ḥijāj* (forehead/head-covering). This is the poet's intended purpose.

*Al-ḥabl* (rope) is that by which things are tied together when one wants them joined to one another, and by which a beast or a prisoner is restrained so that it does not leave its place. It is a twisted cord of fiber or of leather thongs, of varying lengths according to the strength of what is bound or tied to a stake, a ring, or a tree, so that the one tied is prevented from leaving its place for another, to a distance intended. Ships' mooring ropes are also tied to the ground at the shores. It has been mentioned in His saying ﴿and hold fast to the rope of God, all together﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103], and His saying ﴿except by a rope from God and a rope from the people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 112], both in the Surah of Al 'Imran. It is said *ḥabalahu* when he tied it.

*Al-masad* is a strong fiber from Yemeni fiber, and the ropes twisted from it are strong and hard.

The predicate was placed first in His saying ﴿in her neck﴾, for the sake of emphasis on describing that dreadful state in which, in place of the necklace with which she used to adorn her neck in this world, a rope is placed around her neck, when she and her husband were among the wealthy and the chiefs of the people of al-Baṭḥā'. Umm Jamil died in polytheism.

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate

Surah al-Ikhlas

What is well known as its name, in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, in what came from his speech, and in most of what was narrated from the Companions, is (Surah *Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad*).

Al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Hurayra, and Ahmad related from Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari and from Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqba, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "*Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad* equals a third of the Qur'an." This is clear in that he intended to name it by that sentence, because of the feminine pronoun in his saying *(ta'dilu)* (equals), for it refers to it as a surah.

It has also been narrated from a group of Companions what indicates that it is named thus, so that is the name stated in the Sunna.

It is derived from al-Bukhari's hadith, from Ibrahim, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, what indicates that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "*Allahu al-Wahid al-Samad*, is a third of the Qur'an." He mentioned words differing from how it is recited, and its meaning is to be taken as intending the naming. al-Qurtubi mentioned that a man, whom he did not name, recited it in that way while people were listening, and claimed that what he recited was correct. al-Qurtubi censured him and reviled him.

It is named in most of the copies of the Qur'an (*maṣāḥif*), and in most of the exegeses, and in the *Jami'* of al-Tirmidhi, *Surat al-Ikhlas* (the Surah of Sincerity). This name became famous for its brevity and for gathering the meanings of this surah, because in it there is teaching people the sincerity of worship to God Most High, that is, the soundness of belief from associating others with God in divinity.

In some Tunisian copies of the Qur'an it is named *Surat al-Tawhid* (the Surah of Monotheism), because it includes the affirmation that He, Most High, is one.

In *al-Itqan* it is said that it is called *Surat al-Asas* (the Surah of the Foundation), because it includes the Unity of God, and that is

[Page 610]

the foundation of Islam. In *al-Kashshaf* (it was narrated from Ubayy and Anas, from the Prophet ﷺ, that "the seven heavens and the seven earths were founded upon *Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad*"), meaning: they were created only so that they would be signs of the Unity of God and knowledge of His attributes.

It is mentioned in *al-Kashshaf* that it and Surat al-Kafirun are called *al-Muqashqishatan*, that is, the two that free from polytheism and from hypocrisy.

al-Biqa'i in *Nazm al-Durar* named it *Surat al-Samad*, and this is among the names that al-Fakhr (al-Razi) gathered. Al-Fakhr, in *al-Tafsir al-Kabir*, devoted a section to the names of this surah, and mentioned for it twenty names, adding the title "Surah" to each name, and did not mention their chains of transmission. So you should trace them, though they vary. They are: *al-Tafrid* (the Isolation); *al-Tajrid* (the Stripping), because it mentions only His negative attributes, which are the attributes of majesty; *al-Tawhid* (the same reason); *al-Ikhlas* (for what we mentioned just above); *al-Najah* (the Deliverance), because it delivers from disbelief in this world and from the Fire in the Hereafter; *al-Wilaya* (the Guardianship), because whoever knows God by His oneness is among His believing friends who do not take as allies anyone other than God; *al-Nisba* (the Lineage), because it is said that it was revealed when the polytheists said: "Describe for us your Lord," as will come; *al-Ma'rifa* (the Knowledge), because it encompasses the attributes without which the knowledge of God is not complete; *al-Jamal* (the Beauty), because it gathers the roots of God's attributes, which are the most beautiful and most perfect attributes, and because it was narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "God is beautiful and loves beauty," so they asked him about that, and he said: "One, Eternal Refuge; He begets not, nor is He begotten." *Al-Muqashqisha* (it is said: *qashqasha al-dawa'u al-jarab* when the medicine cured the mange, because it cleanses from polytheism; it was previously mentioned that this is also a name of Surat al-Kafirun). *Al-Mu'awwidha* (because of the Prophet's ﷺ saying to 'Uthman ibn Maz'un when he was ill, and he sought refuge for him with it and with the two surahs after it, and said to him: "Seek refuge with them"). *Al-Samad* (because this word is specific to it). *Al-Asas* (because it is the foundation of the Islamic creed). *Al-Mani'a* (the Preventer), because it was narrated that it prevents the punishment of the grave and the blasts of the Fire. *Al-Mahdar* (the Attendance), because the angels attend to listen to it when it is recited. *Al-Munaffira* (the Repeller), because Satan flees at its recitation. *Al-Bara'a* (the Acquittal), because it acquits from polytheism. *Al-Mudhakkira* (the Reminder), because it recalls pure monotheism, which is deposited in the innate nature. *Al-Nur* (the Light), because it was narrated that the light of the Qur'an is *Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad*. *Al-Aman* (the Security), because whoever believes in what it contains is safe from punishment.

[Page 611]

With the addition of its well-known name (*Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad*), its names reach twenty-two. al-Firuzabadi said in *Basa'ir al-Tamyiz* that it is also called *al-Shafiya* (the Healing), which makes twenty-one names.

It is Meccan according to the majority. Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Abu al-'Aliya, and al-Qurazi said: it is Medinan. Both opinions are attributed to Ibn 'Abbas.

The source of this disagreement is the difference over its occasion of revelation. al-Tirmidhi related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, 'Ubayd al-'Attar related from Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu Ya'la related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that "the Quraysh said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'Describe your Lord for us.' So *Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad* was revealed to its end." On this basis it is Meccan.

Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas that "'Amir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad ibn Rabi'a, brother of Labid, came to the Prophet ﷺ. 'Amir said: 'To what do you call us?' He said: 'To God.' He said: 'Describe Him for us: is He of gold, or of silver, or of iron, or of wood?' (He supposed, out of ignorance, that God was an idol like their idols, made of metal, wood or stone.) So this surah was revealed." On this basis it is Medinan, because they came to him only after the Hijra.

al-Wahidi said that the rabbis of the Jews (among them Huyayy ibn Akhtab and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf) said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Describe your Lord for us, perhaps we will believe in you," so it was revealed.

The correct view is that it is Meccan, for it gathers the root of monotheism, which is most of what was revealed of the Qur'an in Mecca. Perhaps the interpretation of those who said it was revealed when 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad asked, or when the rabbis of the Jews asked, is that the Prophet ﷺ recited this surah to them, and the narrator from the Ansar thought it was revealed at that moment, or the narrators did not record their statement with complete accuracy.

In *al-Itqan* it is said: "Some scholars reconciled the two reports by saying it was revealed more than once. Then it became clear to me that it is Medinan, as I explained in *Asbab al-Nuzul*." End of quote.

On the more correct view that it is Meccan, it is counted as the twenty-second surah in the order of revelation, revealed after Surat al-Nas and before Surat al-Najm.

[Page 612]

Its verses, according to the counting scholars of Medina, Kufa, and Basra, are four; according to the scholars of Mecca and Syria they are five, counting ﴿He begets not﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 3] as one verse and ﴿nor is He begotten﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 3] as another.

The affirmation of the Oneness of God Most High.

That none is sought for needs other than Him; His transcendence above the marks of created things; and the refutation that He could have a son.

And the refutation that the one who is born could be God, like Jesus, peace be upon him.

The hadiths on its virtues are numerous, and it is authentically established that it equals a third of the Qur'an. The interpretation of this hadith is mentioned in the commentaries on the *Muwatta'* and the *Two Sahihs*.
